note_tweet.text:
Cannabis is suddenly a national emergency when the person holding it is from the South-East, the North-Central, or a roadside in Ondo with no godfather. When the same substance is reportedly circulating among certain political appointees and big men, the farm suddenly develops selective vision. Executive rascality with a god complex, dressed up as enforcement.

The pigs are in the farmhouse. The rest of us are still outside, being asked to show our papers.

It cuts across every stratum. The Lagos boy with a First Class and Banana Island firm experience moves differently from the boy in Kano or Enugu who has the same degree but no network. The diaspora Nigerian who kept the old friendship warm gets the mandate. The one who stayed home and only has local contacts gets the traffic stop. Church leaders can rewrite bro codes and call it divine while the street gets sermons about morality.

Some animals get grace. Some animals get handcuffs. Some animals get "God be praised" when the deal closes. Others get "why are you travelling at this hour?"

A friendship that began among books became the thread that moved goods across borders. Beautiful. Also, in this country, a reminder that the animals who once shared the same scholarship classroom are still more equal when the real business begins.

The old people said a man who keeps his friend does not walk alone when the road lengthens. They forgot to add that some roads have NDLEA checkpoints and some roads have private jets.

A man who does not know where the rain began to beat him cannot say where he dried his body. We believed in 1960. We believed again and again. We chased Jones away and wrote on the wall: _All animals are equal._

Then the pigs learned to walk on two legs. At first they said it was for the good of the farm. Then they said it was because they needed to read documents. Then they said it was because they were more equal.

Squealer came every evening to explain. He was the town crier who had learned to speak with two mouths. When the law said "No animal shall sleep in a bed," and the pigs were found sleeping in beds, Squealer said, "My brothers, you misheard. The law said no animal shall sleep in a bed _with sheets_."

We laughed. We always laugh when the powerful lie to us, because if we do not laugh, we will cry.

Some Animals Are More Equal: A 2026 Nigerian Adaptation of Animal Farm

They killed Boxer.

Not with gun. Not with knife. With applause.

My name is JO. And if you are planning to clap again in the next election — less than 3 months from now — then this is not a book review for you. Na your obituary.

Yesterday, I casually mentioned a cross-border deal I led. 

What I did not mention is that the mandate did not arrive because I was the most brilliant lawyer in the room.

It arrived because I once walked the same streets and bent over the same books as someone who later decided to float a new entity. We stayed in touch for over a decade. She called. I answered. We closed it.

That is the story.

Or, if we are honest, that is the farm. There is a saying in our land: when the lizard of the house fails to do the things for which the lizard of the bush is praised, the house will fall.

All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others. Some animals get Commonwealth Shared Scholarships and postgraduate certificates in Europe's capital. Some animals keep the thread alive with calls and virtual meetings across oceans. 

Some animals get the call when a new house of trade is being raised. 

Some animals lead the legal team and watch agricultural commodities move from Nigerian farms to UK buyers while the rest of the farm is still arguing about whether the gate is even open.

Meanwhile, on the federal roads, the NDLEA is busy stopping ordinary young men and women whose only crime is that their father is not a Senator and their name does not open doors in Abuja. They search, they embarrass, they delay. 

Cannabis is suddenly a national emergency when the person holding it is from the South-East, the North-Central, or a roadside in Ondo with no godfather. When the same substance is reportedly circulating among certain political appointees and big men, the farm suddenly develops selective vision. Executive rascality with a god complex, dressed up as enforcement.

The pigs are in the farmhouse. The rest of us are still outside, being asked to show our papers.

It cuts across every stratum. The Lagos boy with a First Class and Banana Island firm experience moves differently from the boy in Kano or Enugu who has the same degree but no network. The diaspora Nigerian who kept the old friendship warm gets the mandate. The one who stayed home and only has local contacts gets the traffic stop. Church leaders can rewrite bro codes and call it divine while the street gets sermons about morality.

Some animals get grace. Some animals get handcuffs. Some animals get "God be praised" when the deal closes. Others get "why are you travelling at this hour?"

A friendship that began among books became the thread that moved goods across borders. Beautiful. Also, in this country, a reminder that the animals who once shared the same scholarship classroom are still more equal when the real business begins.

The old people said a man who keeps his friend does not walk alone when the road lengthens. They forgot to add that some roads have NDLEA checkpoints and some roads have private jets.

A man who does not know where the rain began to beat him cannot say where he dried his body. We believed in 1960. We believed again and again. We chased Jones away and wrote on the wall: _All animals are equal._

Then the pigs learned to walk on two legs. At first they said it was for the good of the farm. Then they said it was because they needed to read documents. Then they said it was because they were more equal.

Squealer came every evening to explain. He was the town crier who had learned to speak with two mouths. When the law said "No animal shall sleep in a bed," and the pigs were found sleeping in beds, Squealer said, "My brothers, you misheard. The law said no animal shall sleep in a bed _with sheets_."

We laughed. We always laugh when the powerful lie to us, because if we do not laugh, we will cry.
